entries.title: Can US midterm election really change Trump's Iran policy?
entries.summary: The US midterms are at hand, but their impact on the Iran war remains far from clear. Analysts say the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears.
entries.content:
Asia

Can US midterm election really change Trump's Iran policy?

November 3, 2026

The US midterms are at hand, but their impact on the Iran war remains far from clear. Analysts say the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears.

The US election this Tuesday is shaping up to be one of the most consequential midterm votes in modern US history, with Washington's relationship with Israel and its war on Iran right at the center of the political standoff.

Many Democrats, including the party's rising stars such as Ohio Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, are outspoken critics of the Iran war, with El-Sayed calling the conflict "illegal" and "stupid."

US President Donald Trump sought to downplay the effects of the war during the campaign. Last week, he claimed only "one or two targets" remained in Iran and that those could be settled in 10 minutes. However, he immediately added that messages are still being exchanged, Tehran shows strong interest in a deal, and the US has plenty of time to deal with the crisis.

At the same time, there are reports of the US and Israel preparing to launch a new round of strikes on Iran just after the midterm election and pro-war Republicans such as Senator Ted Cruz are putting pressure on the White House to deal with "the threat" posed by Iran.

"I have urged arming the Iranian protesters to overthrow the regime," Cruz said in an online post after spending a day with Trump.

Behind the scenes, analysts warn that the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears. Moreover, even a resounding Democrat victory might not give them enough leverage on the Trump administration regarding the Iran war.

Democrats and Republicans broadly 'in consensus' on Iran

Talking to DW, former National Security Advisor John Bolton said the Democrats are likely to secure a majority in the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate, handing them control of the Iran war funding.

The US Congress "can allocate defense budgets or impose restrictions on the use of financial resources," Bolton said.

Nevertheless, Bolton points out that the US president can veto congressional legislation, which would then require a two-thirds majority in both assemblies to overcome.

"Even if Democrats hold a majority in both houses, their influence will be limited to the legislative and political tools of Congress," he said.

US diplomat and Iran expert Alan Eyre points to a kind of "bipartisan consensus" that Republicans and Democrats have on Iran.

"Both major US parties share significant common ground in their opposition to the political structure of the Islamic Republic and in their support for policies aimed at exerting pressure on Tehran to change its behavior," he said.

What does Tehran think?

While warning of a "crushing response" to any new strikes on underground sites, Tehran has confirmed ongoing indirect communication via Doha and Muscat, keeping its diplomatic option open.

Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst leading the Iran team at ITSS Verona, told DW that Tehran's actions are based on a miscalculation. The regime, he argues, assumes that a Democratic Congress can easily restrain the White House.

Tehran's strategy in dragging out peace talks, pressuring the Strait of Hormuz, and letting fuel prices weigh on US voters, aims to deny Trump a win before November. However, Modarres notes this strategy may backfire after the election, as the Trump administration will no longer have any reason to delay its moves.

This approach also ignores the fact that both US parties largely agree on not letting Iranian develop nuclear weapons, he said.

Will Trump launch new strikes and declare victory?

Trump's ally-turned-critic John Bolton believes that Trump will only decide on his next steps on Iran after the election, once the political pressure grows less acute.

"I cannot predict what the US President will do; even Trump himself does not know his final decision right now," he told DW.

Bolton cites as an example a possible US attack on "Kuh-e Kolang," the new nuclear site he claims the Iranian government is constructing near Natanz.

"In this scenario, Trump could damage these facilities, declare victory, and pull back."

Bolton: 'Regime change' only guarantee against Iran getting nukes

Trump has consistently emphasized that the US goal is to deny Iran the capability of acquiring nuclear weapons. Throughout the conflict, the US president has also repeatedly claimed his administration had succeeded in this regard.

Bolton, in contrast, believes that the Islamic Republic will continue to pursue nuclear weapons capability for as long as it remains in power.

The former Trump advisor views "regime change" as the only sustainable solution to keep Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.

US failing to communicate with ordinary Iranians

Eyre, the first Persian-speaking diplomat to be the spokesperson for the US Department of State, emphasizes the difficulty of using external tools to bring about sustainable change. In his view, even if there is a consensus in Washington opposing the Islamic Republic and demanding a change in its behavior, this US consensus alone cannot overcome the structural obstacles to political change inside Iran. He reiterates that any fundamental transformation must emerge from within Iranian society itself.

The veteran diplomat also points to the failure of "Washington's public diplomacy to convey a clear, coherent, and authentic message to Iranian society."

He notes that official US government messaging is only incompletely reflected in the media outlets that the vast majority of Iranian citizens rely on for news.

"Furthermore, targeted and principled engagement with the core of Iranian society has generally not been a priority for successive US administrations," he said.

"Iranian citizens see that the US takes certain positions at the rhetorical level, but behaves differently in practice."

According to Eyre, this gap between words and deeds in Washington is a structural phenomenon that is not limited to a single administration or a single election cycle.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Football: Spanish player dies on after cardiac arrest on the pitch
entries.summary: Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel has died following a collision with the opposing goalkeeper. The Spanish second division club has said it is "heartbroken" at the loss.
entries.content:
Spain

Football: Spanish player dies after on-pitch collision

November 3, 2026

Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel has died following a collision with the opposing goalkeeper. The Spanish second division club has said it is "heartbroken" at the loss.

"Heartbroken with pain, with a lump in our throat and unable to believe this is real." Those were the words with which Spanish second division football club Tenerife confirmed the death of their 30-year-old player, Jesus de Miguel, on Tuesday.

De Miguel, 30, was involved in a clash in the middle of the pitch with FC Andorra's  Equatorial Guinea international goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who had raced out of his goal to try and clear the ball with the score 2-2 late in the game. Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.

Spanish media said that De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest and was resuscitated. The player was taken to hospital and placed in intensive care, with Tenerife later saying that De Miguel's condition had "worsened neurologically", before his death.

After confirming the death on Tuesday morning, the club posted that: "No words can ease the pain, nothing can lessen this great feeling of sadness. Our thoughts are with the family, his close friends and Tenerife fans, who today are grieving over this terrible news."

Andorra also sent their "most sincere condolences" as messages of support began to flood in on Tuesday.

"I am so deeply sorry. Rest in peace, Jesus," former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, Andorra's majority shareholder, wrote on social media.

Real Madrid, Barcelona, Atletico Madrid and other clubs in Spain also sent messages of condolence, as well as the Spanish FA (RFEF).

"Shattered by this sad news, the Royal Spanish Football Federation wishes to express our deepest sorrow at his passing today," wrote the federation in a statement.

The RFEF postponed Tuesday's matches in the Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina, "as a gesture of respect and solidarity."

De Miguel had been with Tenerife since joining from from Castellon in 2025. He began his career with Leganes at youth level in the Madrid suburbs, playing for a string of teams, including Unionistas de Salamanca, before signing for Castellon in 2023.

entries.title: Zelenskyy arrives in Berlin for talks with Merz on air defense and energy support ahead of US-led negotiations with Russia
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Berlin for talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Kyiv is seeking more air defense missiles and help keeping its energy system running through winter.
entries.content:
Germany

Ukraine's Zelenskyy arrives in Berlin for talks with Merz

November 3, 2026

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Berlin for talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Kyiv is seeking more air defense missiles and help keeping its energy system running through winter.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Berlin on Tuesday for talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on strengthening support for Ukraine.

Kyiv is seeking more air-defense hardware to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, as well as support for its energy sector ahead of winter. The visit comes a week before US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi.

What is on the agenda in Berlin?

"The key issues are our diplomatic coordination — with important meetings ahead — strengthening our air defence, and supporting our energy sector," Zelenskyy wrote on X.

His visit came hours after Russia launched a large overnight attack on Ukraine using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. At least 73 people were injured in a strike on a hospital in the eastern city of Kharkiv, regional prosecutors said. They said 226 patients had to be transferred to other hospitals.

Ukraine needs interceptors for air defense systems such as the US-made Patriot. Germany, one of Ukraine's biggest military, financial and humanitarian supporters, says it has already supplied all the Patriot systems it can spare without weakening its own air defenses.

Zelenskyy told EU leaders in October that Ukraine would need an additional €70 billion ($78 billion) from European governments next year. Germany plans to host a summit of countries backing Ukraine in mid-November to discuss further support ahead of winter.

How has Berlin stepped up security?

The visit coincides with the opening of the two-day Berlin Security Conference, which brings together European officials and defense experts. Russia's war in Ukraine is high on the agenda.

Police said about 3,400 additional officers were deployed for the visit and the conference, with reinforcements from across Germany.

Armed officers guarded barriers around parts of the government district, and special police units deployed snipers. Roads were also closed in western Berlin, including near the Kurfürstendamm shopping avenue.

How does the visit fit into the peace talks?

US special envoy Steve Witkoff said advisers from Ukraine, Russia and the United States would meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 to discuss postwar security, steps to reduce tensions and humanitarian aid.

US envoys are due to discuss security guarantees and reconstruction with European and NATO representatives in Brussels this week. Berlin expects European representatives to be in Abu Dhabi, though they are unlikely to have a seat at the negotiating table.

entries.title: Asian Cup postponed due to Middle East conflict
entries.summary: The Asian Cup has become the latest sporting event to be affected by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Organizers cite "exceptional circumstances" in Saudi Arabia, which has seen several Houthi attacks of late.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Asian Cup postponed due to Middle East conflict

November 3, 2026

The Asian Cup has become the latest sporting event to be affected by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Organizers cite "exceptional circumstances" in Saudi Arabia, which has seen several Houthi attacks of late.

A little over two months before it was set to kick off, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed its flagship international football tournament in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country, Saudi Arabia.

The AFC cited "substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions" caused by conflicts in the region.

Instead of January 7, 2027, the tournament will now kick off on December 23 and end on January 21, 2028. The postponement follows delays and cancellations of a number of sporting events in the region, including a Formula One race, the men's and women's tennis finals, the 2027 Dakar Rally and disruption to Asia's marquee continental club football tournament, the AFC Champions League Elite.

Saudi Arabia hosted, and won, the Gulf Cup last month, but there had already been much talk about whether the much larger Asian Cup could go ahead. 

Houthi attacks make tournament impossible

It was scheduled to feature 24 teams playing matches in eight venues across Riyadh, Jeddah and Khobar. However, the AFC said that "circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," made the tournament impossible. 

"Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organization and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders."

In particular, the postponement was forced by a recent wave of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi rebels as well as other raging conflicts in the region. The Houthis have targeted Saudi infrastructure, including airports. They are fighting a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government, a civil war that reignited in July following a years-long truce.

The AFC had been under pressure from several federations to postpone the tournament, with South Korea's players leading the way.

Player and fan safety comes first

"The ongoing military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that cannot be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, president of the Korea Professional Footballers Association, said last month, according to the Yonhap News Agency.

Lee added that "no tournament's value can take precedence over the lives and safety of players and football fans."

It seems that the AFC now agrees. However, following the announcement of the postponement, Yasser al-Misehal, chairman of the local organizing committee, promised that Saudi Arabia was "fully ready" whenever the tournament ended up being held.

"The tournament will move to the new dates, and our preparations will continue as planned," he told the Saudi Press Agency.

"We're working closely with the AFC and all our partners to make sure the tournament runs smoothly and meets the high standards expected of Saudi Arabia and the Asian Cup."

Saudi sports investments dwindling with World Cup on horizon

Saudi Arabia has invested hugely in sports over the last decade, from owning Premier League teams to hosting boxing title fights and bidding for a number of major sporting events, most notably World Cup 2034, which they won the right to host unopposed.

However, the country has recently withdrawn or slashed funding for a number of sporting events including golf, rugby, tennis and winter sports.

entries.title: How AI giants could raise the cost of borrowing in Europe
entries.summary: France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.
entries.content:
November 3, 2026

France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.

With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google-owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued around $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.

Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.

Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

Battle for investor capital heats up

That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.

The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."

That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

'Bond abundance' helps drive up yields

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.

Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.

European companies could also feel more pain

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.

The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.

Regional governments paying the price for AI

The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned. 

The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

entries.title: US midterms: Americans vote in polls seen as referendum on Trump
entries.summary: The crucial midterms will determine how much power President Donald Trump has to make changes in the last two years of his term. Follow DW's live updates.
entries.content:
United States of America

US midterms: Americans vote in polls seen as referendum on Trump

Published November 3, 2026last updated November 3, 2026

The crucial midterms will determine how much power President Donald Trump has to make changes in the last two years of his term. Follow DW's live updates.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The first polls opened at 5 a.m. local time (1000 GMT) in Vermont
  • Voters are electing all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate
  • Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republicans
  • Polls suggest the Democrats have a good chance of taking control of the House, but the battle for the Senate is tighter
  • The party holding the White House typically sees losses in the midterms

Follow the latest developments from the US midterm elections on November 3, 2026:

Skip next section WATCH — Democrat backs Republican in Michigan Senate race shock

WATCH — Democrat backs Republican in Michigan Senate race shock

Former Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens, who lost to nominee Abdul El-Sayed in the primary, has endorsed Republican Mike Rogers, shaking up one of America's most crucial Senate races.

Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republican Party in Tuesday's midterms, with the Michigan race a key battleground that could help them flip control of the Senate.

Skip next section When can we expect results?

When can we expect results?

The first results will likely start arriving on Tuesday evening after polls begin to close, but it could take hours or even days for the outcome of some closely contested races to become clear.

The first polling stations close in Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. local time (2300 GMT), followed by Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia one hour later.

Votes cast on election day are often processed before mail-in ballots, which means the overall result can shift significantly as the count progresses.

Results will come in throughout Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning as states release their vote counts.

US media outlets may start to make calls and projections based on exit polls and early counts from state election officials.

Several outlets, including DW, rely on the Associated Press for race calls.

In 2022, the Senate results weren't finalized until four days after the election, while for the House of Representatives results it took eight days. In the midterms before that, the outcome was already clear on election night.

Skip next section IN DEPTH — Why the midterms matter and which races to watch

IN DEPTH — Why the midterms matter and which races to watch

US citizens are voting in Tuesday's midterms for who they want to see in the Capitol.

Midterm elections are held every four years, at the exact halfway point between presidential elections. The people of the United States decide who will represent them in the two chambers of the US Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate. Some states are also voting for their governor. These are the decisions on the ballot paper — but they are not the only thing voters will be taking into account.

J. Miles Coleman, an election analyst at the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, explained before the last midterms that they were "often a referendum on the president and party currently in power."

If the people are content, the party of the leader in the White House does better than if the people are predominantly dissatisfied. President Donald Trump's approval ratings are currently at a record low.

Read more here about what that means and which races to watch.

Skip next section Voting kicks off in US midterm elections

Voting kicks off in US midterm elections

The first polling stations opened at 5 a.m. (1000 GMT) in the eastern US state of Vermont for the midterm elections.

Voting is to follow in Connecticut, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Missouri, New Jersey, New York and Virginia from 6 a.m. local time. And polls open in West Virginia, North Carolina and Ohio at 6:30 a.m.

More than 57 million ballots were cast early in 47 states and Washington DC as of Monday. Many more votes will be cast in person on Tuesday.

Polling stations across the country close between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m., with vote counting beginning immediately afterwards.

Skip next section What happened on the final day of campaigning?

What happened on the final day of campaigning?

Democratic candidates were pushing their message in the key Republican strongholds of Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Kansas as campaigning wrapped up on Monday, seeking to capitalize on voter dissatisfaction with the Iran war and rising prices.

Republicans, meanwhile, cast their opponents as left-wing radicals while touting President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown and tax cuts as policies that will benefit Americans.

In his final public campaign appearance at the National Mall, Trump appeared to lower expectations for his party's performance.

"For some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot," he said, adding that the Democrats had "nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history."

In rambling remarks, he said little about the national economy, only insisting that it was "great." Instead, he devoted most of his speech to the renovation of Washington's algae-plagued Reflecting Pool.

Vice President JD Vance campaigned in Rome, New York, praising Trump's moves to end taxes on tips and overtime and secure the border while calling Democrats as "lunatics."

In Texas, which hasn't had a Democratic senator since 1988, Democrat James Talarico blamed Trump's "corrupt tariffs" for rising grocery prices and "a new corrupt war in the Middle East" for higher gas and diesel prices.

In the same state, Republican Ken Paxton attacked Talarico in cultural terms as "a vegan who hates meat," and falsely calling him a democratic socialist "just like New York Mayor Mamdani."

Meanwhile, in the key state of Michigan, Democrats were working to maintain a united front after a messy spat that culminated in Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens endorsing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

El-Sayed largely ignored the controversy at campaign events on Monday, stressing instead that his campaign was about the concerns of voters.

Stevens did not attend Rogers' rally Monday night, but she got a long ovation from the crowd when Rogers mentioned her endorsement.

Skip next section US strikes Iran on eve of midterms

US strikes Iran on eve of midterms

The US carried out strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on the eve of crucial midterm elections, according to reports.

"Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets" were targeted, a US official was quoted by the Associated Press as saying.

Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island, which is located in the Strait of Hormuz.   

The US Central Command did not officially confirm the attack.

The strikes came as US President Donald Trump's Republican Party seeks to retain control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections. The outcome of the polls will determine how much power Trump has for the remainder of his term.

Trump's popularity has taken a dive, partly in response to the Iran war and its impact on US gas prices. He had previously said the US wouldn't launch new strikes on Iran before the midterms.

The attack came after Tehran said on Monday it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the US if Washington meets its demands, including lifting a blockade of Iranian ports.

Trump wrote on social media on Monday that a deal with Tehran "could happen."

Vice President JD Vance also told reporters that he had spoken to Trump about talks with Iran and said that "the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from the DW newsroom in Bonn!

Voters in the US are heading to the polls for midterm elections that are set to shape US President Donald Trump's last two years in office.

Americans are electing all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate. Many states are also holding votes to elect local representatives.

The midterms, held around the halfway mark of a presidential term, are typically seen as a referendum on the president's policies. In almost every modern midterm election, the party in the White House has lost seats in Congress.

This year, Democrats are widely expected to retake the House but could face a greater challenge in the Senate.

If the Republicans lose control of either chamber, Trump's power will be curbed for the remainder of his term. That would also open the door for the Democrats to investigate his administration. If Democrats win a majority in the Senate, they could also block Trump's nominations for federal courts.    

More than 57 million Americans cast their ballots early, but on Tuesday many more US citizens will vote in person.

Stay tuned as we bring you the latest developments from the midterms in our live blog.

entries.title: US midterm election: How it works, why it's important and races to watch
entries.summary: US voters are electing a new Congress. The results will be decisive for the future of the United States, and a judgment on Donald Trump's second term as president.
entries.content:
United States of America

US midterm election: Why it's important and races to watch

November 3, 2026

US voters are electing a new Congress. The results will be decisive for the future of the United States, and a judgment on Donald Trump's second term as president.

On November 3, United States citizens will vote in the midterm elections. These won't decide who gets to sit in the White House; instead, Americans will be voting on who they want to see in the Capitol.

Midterm elections are held every four years, at the exact halfway point between presidential elections. The people of the United States decide who will represent them in the two chambers of the US Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate. Some states are also voting for their governor. These are the decisions on the ballot paper — but they are not the only thing voters will be taking into account.

J. Miles Coleman, an election analyst at the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, explained before the last midterms that they were "often a referendum on the president and party currently in power." If the people are content, the party of the leader in the White House does better than if the people are predominantly dissatisfied. President Donald Trump's approval ratings are currently at a record low.

Who are Americans electing in the midterms?

All the seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election. Its 435 members are elected by eligible voters across the country. Each member represents one electoral district. These are allocated based on population size. As a result, relatively large US states where few people live, such as Wyoming, have only one seat in the House of Representatives. New Jersey, a much smaller state by surface area but with a larger population, has 12. Representatives are elected for a two-year term of office.

US senators, on the other hand, are elected for a six-year term. The Senate, the other chamber of the US Congress, has 100 seats: two for each of the 50 US states, regardless of size. Around one third of these senatorial seats come up for election every two years. This year there are 35, meaning that not every state will be electing a senator in these midterms.

Separately, voters in 36 states will elect their governor, whose term of office is four years in most states. Many decisions in the US are taken at state level, on everything from abortion law to education and electoral procedure. It can therefore make a considerable difference to people's lives whether Democrats or Republicans are the ones making these decisions in their state.

Who currently has a majority in the US Congress?

At present, the Republicans, the party of President Trump, have a majority in both houses of Congress — but its margin is slim.

The House of Representatives currently has 218 Republican deputies, 214 Democrats, and one independent, who usually votes with the Republicans. Two seats are vacant. Observers think it likely that the Democrats will seize the majority in this chamber in the upcoming elections. "It would be a surprise if the Democrats don't at least take the House [of Representatives]," Coleman told the American broadcaster CBS at the end of October.

In the Senate there are currently 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and two independent senators who usually vote with the Democrats. When a vote in the Senate is deadlocked 50:50, the US vice president has the deciding vote. This means that currently, Trump's Vice President JD Vance would tip the scales if there were a tie in a Senate vote.

Why are the midterms so important?

Voter turnout is typically lower for midterms than for presidential elections, but the results will decisively influence US politics for the next few years. Despite the significant executive power delegated to the presidency, the majority of federal political decisions have to be approved by Congress before they can be implemented.

It is therefore considerably easier for Trump to govern the country as he chooses if the Republicans have a majority in both chambers of Congress. If the Democrats win a majority in one or both chambers, it will be more difficult for him to make changes to either domestic or foreign policy.

Which races are crucial?

The Democrats only need to win four more seats in the House of Representatives to gain a majority. They would then have 218 representatives. Out of the 435 races, only a few are still considered toss-ups. These include districts in Iowa, Virginia and Montana.

One senatorial race to watch is the one in Texas. Current polls put Democrat James Talarico level with his Republican rival, Ken Paxton. The Democrats need four more seats in the Senate to win a majority. The possibility that Texas could be one of them is already a sensation. No Democrat has won here at state level since 1994. Talarico now even has the support of some members of the Bush family, the Texas Republican dynasty of former presidents George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush, his son.

In the gubernatorial elections it is possible that, for the first time in US history, a Black woman could become state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the Black Republican Lisa DeMuth are vying for the position, while in Georgia the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is up against the Republican Rick Jackson.

DeMuth is unlikely to win in Minnesota: The state generally votes Democrat, and Klobuchar, who has been state senator there for almost two decades, is much better known than her rival. In Georgia, however, the latest polls suggest it's neck-and-neck. Bottoms has a realistic chance of winning.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Germany news: Ukraine in focus at Berlin Security Conference
entries.summary: A security conference in the German capital is to examine ways of defending against threats from Russia. The justice minister has put forward a bill that would raise penalties for sexual offenses. DW has more.

Germany

Germany news: Ukraine in focus at Berlin Security Conference

Published November 3, 2026last updated November 3, 2026

A security conference in the German capital is to examine ways of defending against threats from Russia. The justice minister has put forward a bill that would raise penalties for sexual offenses. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The 25th Berlin Security Conference is kicking off in the German capital, with Lithuania as this year's partner country
  • The conference will focus on the war in Ukraine and ways to counter growing Russian aggression against European countries
  • Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig has presented a bill that broadens the definition of sexual harassment and envisages higher penalties for sexual offenses
  • Conservative Bavarian Premier Markus Söder has called for a European-Arab free trade area during a trip to the United Arab Emirates
  • Another child has been reported injured by a sharp object hidden in Halloween candy

This is a roundup of some of the top stories from and about Germany on November 3, 2026:

Skip next section New gas-fired plants to be built as wind and solar energy backup

New gas-fired plants to be built as wind and solar energy backup

New gas-fired power stations are to be built across Germany by 2031 to supply electricity to the grid when wind and solar generation is not sufficient, according to plans announced by the Federal Network Agency on Tuesday.

The projects were selected through a tender process in which 41 bids were submitted.

Eleven of those were successful, with 10 going to energy giants RWE and LEAG or their affiliates.

The average contract price was said to be €155,296 ($173,829) per megawatt-hour, which results in annual costs of just over €800 million for the 11 power station projects.

Those costs are to be borne by all electricity consumers via a new levy that will raise prices, though it remains unclear by how much.

Initially, the new plants will be fired by natural gas, but it is planned that they will use climate-neutral hydrogen by 2045 at the latest.

The environmental organization Greenpeace has criticized the plan, saying that the government "continues to chain our country" to fossil fuel.

It said modern, environmentally friendly and increasingly cheap alternatives such as energy storage systems had been excluded from the first tender process.

The conservative Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche has faced much criticism over her ties to the energy sector, her former field of work. 

Skip next section Merz reports progress on bill to stop Berlin Left's expropriation scheme

Merz reports progress on bill to stop Berlin Left's expropriation scheme

A bill that aims to prevent the Left Party from putting large private housing companies into public ownership in Berlin if it comes to power is making progress, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday.

"The bill is finished," Merz, the leader of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU),said at an event organized by the Berlin Chamber of Industry and Commerce.

He said the only open question was whether 100% or 80% of the market value had to be compensated.

"I don't think I need to spell out that we favor 100% market value," he said.

His remarks come as the socialist Left Party, which emerged as strongest force in state elections in Berlin in September, is holding coalition talks with the Greens and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).

Move to reduce cost of rentals

An exploratory paper issued by the three parties includes plan to expropriate private housing companies with holdings of at least 10,000 apartments in Berlin, with some compensation also planned, though critics say it is too little.

The Left Party argues that offering the then state-owned apartments at lower rents would have a knock-on effect, reducing prices across Berlin.

Merz, for his part, said that such an expropriation in the German capital would have negative "repercussions as far as the capital markets in London, Paris and New York," saying that protecting property was a basic principle underpinning the economic order.

He said seizing companies in this way would severely damage the business environment, while failing to create jobs or housing.

However, it is in doubt whether the federal government can legally ban the planned expropriation, with Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig from the SPD among those expressing doubts about a general prohibition.

Skip next section Another child injured eating Halloween candy

Another child injured eating Halloween candy

A second child has received slight mouth injuries after eating manipulated candy collected at Halloween, police in the northeastern city of Rostock said on Tuesday.

The child was said to have bitten on a needle hidden in the candy.

This comes after a 9-year-old girl in Bremervörde in the state of Lower Saxony also suffered injuries to her tongue from a 5-cm (2-inch) pin contained in a chocolate bar.

Police in several other states have also reported finds of sharp metal items in Halloween candy, with parents warned to carefully examine treats collected during trick-and-treating on October 31.

It remains unclear how the items came to be in the candy, but police are looking into the possibility that intentional physical harm was in play.

Skip next section Bavarian Premier Söder calls for European-Arab free trade zone

Bavarian Premier Söder calls for European-Arab free trade zone

Markus Söder, the leader of Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and premier of the southern state, has said Europe should establish a free trade area with Arab countries.

On the sidelines of a visit to the United Arab Emirates, Söder, whose party is allied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), said, "I believe that further free trade areas are needed to facilitate all the investments that can be made there."

He said other Arab countries other than the Emirates would also be interested.

In September, the Emirati head of state, Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, announced investments worth up to tens of billions in Germany during a state visit, with €10 billion ($11.1 billion) intended for Bavaria.

Söder is to visit Qatar on Tuesday as part of his trip.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Ukraine's Zelenskyy to visit Berlin for talks

IN DEPTH: Ukraine's Zelenskyy to visit Berlin for talks

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has announced that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will pay a surprise visit to Berlin on Tuesday.

The visit, which was kept secret for security reasons, comes as Zelenskyy is demanding more help from European allies to help defend his country against Russia's invasion as the US proves increasingly unreliable in this regard.

You can read more in this DW article: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy to make surprise Berlin visit this Tuesday, Merz says

Skip next section First supermarket freezer attacks reported in Germany

First supermarket freezer attacks reported in Germany

Several media outlets are reporting that hacking attacks have targeted freezers in German supermarkets for the first time, causing them to heat up to 50 C (122 F) and thus damaging the food they contain.

One reported attack was at a supermarket in Lower Bavaria in southern Germany, while others were said to have occurred in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

In one case, the attack was reportedly not directly on the supermarket concerned, but on the company that monitored the freezer systems remotely.

The attacks follow similar incidents in several other European countries, including France, Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden.

So far, authorities have failed to identify the person or people responsible for the attacks.

Skip next section Justice Minister Hubig presents bill on sexual offenses

Justice Minister Hubig presents bill on sexual offenses

A new bill put forward by Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig envisages tightening law on sexual offenses, among other things by criminalizing verbal sexual harassment and raising penalties for gang rapes.

According to the bill, "anyone harassing another person with a sexually meant utterance or gesture that could intimidate or pressure them" could face criminal charges.

The bill thus seeks to make "catcalling" an offense, although the bill does not use this term, as Hubig's ministry argues that the word is controversial and trivializes the act.

The draft legislation would also make gang rapes punishable by a prison sentence of no fewer than five years, while sexual assaults or sexual coercion carried out by several perpetrators would bring a minimum sentence of three years rather than the current two.

Under the provisions of the bill, limitation periods would also be set uniformly at 20 years for gang rapes and sexual assaults.

Currently, the period can be as short as five years in some cases.

"Sexual harassment and sexualized violence are a massive problem and are part of everyday life for too many woman," Hubig said.

She said "red lines and punishments" were needed to make offenders realize that "sexual offenses are unacceptable," whether physical or verbal in character.

"No matter whether at home, online or on the street and squares — women have to be safe from assault," she said.

Skip next section Berlin Security Conference kicks off

Berlin Security Conference kicks off

The two-day Berlin Security Conference is kicking off in the German capital for the 25th time on Tuesday.

This year, the focus will be on what many see as the biggest challenge toRussia's war in Ukraine European peace for decades: the threat of Russian aggression as reflected in its invasion of Ukraine and hybrid attacks on other European countries.

The conference's partner country this year is Lithuania, a country that shares an uncomfortable border with Russia and fears greatly for its own security.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda is to open the event and later to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, with not just security issues but also Lithuania's upcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union on the agenda.

The program for the conference also includes a speech by a still unnamed "special guest" to be held mid-morning.

The conference has been taking place annually since 2001.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the banks of the still-languishing Rhine River in Bonn!

Today, we will be looking at what comes out of this year's Berlin Security Conference, where European lawmakers, military figures and security authorities will discuss the threat emanating from Russia as it continues its invasion of Ukraine.

We will also focus on a bill envisaging a wider definition of what constitutes a sexual offense and harsher penalties for those guilty of perpetrating them.

And there has been another report of a child's being injured from eating Halloween candy.

You can read about these stories and more in our updates from the heart of Europe.

India news: Cyclone Murasu wreaks havoc after landfall

Published November 3, 2026last updated November 3, 2026

Cyclone Murasu made landfall in Andhra Pradesh, leaving a trail of destruction. Weather agencies have warned of heavy rainfall in the next 12 hours. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Due to the cyclone, schools have been closed in at least eight districts of Andhra Pradesh as a precautionary measure
  • Locals are protesting the felling of thousands of trees on the west coast in Maharashtra's Karjat city
  • Indian navy rescued Iranian crew from pirates

Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from across India on Tuesday, November 3.

Skip next section Thank you for reading

Thank you for reading

That is all for today. We will be back with more news from India tomorrow.

Skip next section Andhra Pradesh: NDA confident of win in civic body elections

Andhra Pradesh: NDA confident of win in civic body elections

The National Democratic Alliance (NDA) is seemingly set for a sweeping victory in Andhra Pradesh municipal elections that were held in 92 urban districts across the state.

The elections are an important contest between the ruling NDA coalition, comprising the Telugu Desam Party, Jana Sena Party and the Bharatiya Janata Party, and the Opposition Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party (YSRCP), often shortened to simply the YSR Congress Party.

The NDA nominees are leading in almost all municipal corporations and a majority of municipalities in the state.

The NDA is expected to win more than 90% of the wards/divisions in urban civic bodies.

The state's civic poll is being seen as a political test for the NDA led by Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu. The result of the civic polls is also expected to offer an indication of the YSR Congress Party's popularity in the state's urban areas.

Skip next section Over 4,000 evicted in Assam after homes of Bengali Muslim families bulldozed

Over 4,000 evicted in Assam after homes of Bengali Muslim families bulldozed

More than 4,000 people were evicted in the northeastern state of Assam after authorities demolished homes during an eviction drive, officials told Indian media outlet Scroll.

The demolition drive took place in Assam's Dhubri district's Alamganj Part-IX village. Local media reported that most of the 4,000 displaced people were Bengali Muslims.

Citing Dhubri District Commissioner Dibakar Nath, Scroll reported that eviction notices had been served to residents occupying 500 acres of land. Authorities evicted the families, claiming it was government land under encroachment.

Nath claimed that residents had settled on the government land in different phases, with some arriving five years ago and others a decade ago. "Most of them have land in other places," he alleged.

However, residents have disputed this claim. Several families reportedly had been paying land revenue for years.

Over the past few years, eviction drives have become more frequent in Assam, under the Hindu-nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party-led government.

In the last ten years of BJP rule in Assam, around 19,000 families, the majority of them Muslim, have been evicted from government land, according to data from the state revenue and disaster management department and the district authorities compiled by Scroll.

Skip next section Amit Shah says 30 million deleted voters were 'Bangladeshi infiltrators'

Amit Shah says 30 million deleted voters were 'Bangladeshi infiltrators'

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Monday claimed that 30 million of the 130 million voters removed from the electoral rolls during the mass voter roll revisions were "Bangladeshi infiltrators," without offering further evidence.

Speaking at a rally in Hyderabad, Shah said, "Thirty million votes were those who never existed," Shah claimed. "These votes were those of Bangladeshi infiltrators…Tell me whether these votes should be cut or not?"

Doubling down on his attack on the opposition alliance INDIA bloc, Shah said the INDIA bloc rally held in Delhi on Sunday was not to save votes but to save infiltrators who form the vote bank of "Congress and company."

"The Congress party wants to capture elections through bogus voting," Shah alleged.

The opposition in India has been pushing back against the mass voter deletions and demanding the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar, alleging his role in deliberate voter deletions favoring Shah's Bharatiya Janata Party.

Skip next section Indian Navy rescues crew members from hijacked Iranian ship

Indian Navy rescues crew members from hijacked Iranian ship

The Indian Navy coordinated a 48-hour operation and rescued 20 crew members from the Iranian fishing vessel Azini after it was hijacked by armed pirates off the coast of Somalia.

In response, the Indian Navy tasked a mission-deployed warship to intervene, supported by a maritime reconnaissance aircraft.

The vessel was seized by Somali pirates on October 29.

According to officials, the operation was carried out 3,000 km from Mumbai in the Arabian Sea.

"Executing a swift and well-coordinated tactical intervention, the Indian Navy secured the vessel, overcame the pirate threat and ensured the safe release of all 20 crew members," the Navy said.

Iran thanked the Indian government for rescuing the crew.

"The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in New Delhi expresses its sincere appreciation to the Government of India, the Indian Navy and the Indian Air Force for their successful operation to rescue the 20 Iranian crew members of the fishing vessel Azini from pirates," the Iranian mission said in a post on social media.

Skip next section Indian tourist dies as two helicopters collide mid-air in Nepal

Indian tourist dies as two helicopters collide mid-air in Nepal

An Indian tourist was killed and three others were injured after two helicopters crashed into each other while landing in Nepal's Solukhumbu district on Tuesday morning.

According to the Hindustan Times, which cited local officials, the Indian tourist was from Tamil Nadu's Chennai and identified as Vasanth Kumar Balaramaramadu (47).

Nepalese pilots Rabindra Prajapati of Fishtail Air and Prajwal KC of Dynasty Air were also injured in the incident and have been taken to Kathmandu for further treatment.

The helicopters were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking up to the Mount Everest base camp during Nepal's popular trekking season.

Reportedly, the incident took place at Pheriche village, which is at 4,200 meters (13,780 feet) altitude.

Skip next section Karjat residents protest tree felling for proposed power plant project

Karjat residents protest tree felling for proposed power plant project

Residents in the Maharashtrian city of Karjat, which lies on the west coast, are pushing back against the large-scale tree felling for a proposed 3,000-MW pumped storage power plant in the region.

More than 32,000 trees are expected to be cleared for construction. According to a report by the Indian Express, nearly 1,100 trees were cut down before the operation was halted last week amid protests.

On Monday, a demonstration by residents, political groups, and environmental activists prompted an almost total shutdown of activity in Karjat.

The hydropower project is being built by Torrent Power is expected to be operational by 2029.

The project needs 377 hectares of land along the Sahyadri range in Raigad district and is expected to cut Maharashtra’s dependence on coal-fired power.

However, environmental experts have warned against the clearing of the forest on the west coast, warning it will disrupt the moisture cycles that bring rain to regions far away.

Skip next section Heavy rains batter coastal Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Murasu makes landfall

Heavy rains batter coastal Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Murasu makes landfall

Severe cyclonic storm 'Murasu' began its landfall close to Ongole in the Prakasam district of the coastal state of Andhra Pradesh during the early hours on Tuesday.

The cyclone, which, according to the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD), is currently moving towards the north-northwest, has left a trail of destruction in the region.

Packing strong winds with heavy rains, the cyclone reportedly has uprooted thousands of trees and damaged electric poles and crops in the coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh.

Schools and colleges have been closed in at least eight districts in Andhra Pradesh as a precautionary measure in view of the heavy rainfall and strong winds.

Heavy spells of rainfall were also likely across south coastal Andhra Pradesh during the next 12 hours, IMD said.

The cyclone is currently over the west central Bay of Bengal close to the south Andhra Pradesh coast and is likely to weaken gradually into a cyclonic storm by noon and further into a deep depression by Tuesday midnight.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Midhat from DW's New Delhi Bureau, bringing you the biggest headlines from India.

After Cyclone Arnab, Cyclone Murasu has brought heavy rainfall and strong winds to the southern state of Andhra Pradesh on the east coast, disrupting life in the region.

Meanwhile, residents are protesting the planned felling of thousands of trees in the city of Karjat in the Maharashtra state on the west coast. A total of 32,000 trees are planned to be cleared for a pumped storage power plant.

At sea, the Indian Navy managed to rescue 20 Iranian crew members from Somali pirates in a coordinated 48-hour operation.

Stay tuned as we bring you more updates from India.

entries.title: North Korea denies role in record Binance hack, calls US charge 'provocation'
entries.summary: Kim Yo Jong dismissed FBI claims that North Korean hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, as the exchange began reopening withdrawals on more networks.
entries.content:
November 3, 2026

Kim Yo Jong dismissed FBI claims that North Korean hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, as the exchange began reopening withdrawals on more networks.

North Korea has hit back at US accusations that its hackers drained more than $6 billion (more than 5.36 billion euros) from cryptocurrency exchange Binance. Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, called the charge "a grave political provocation," according to state media agency KCNA.

Kim described the US claim as "absurd rhetoric and nothing new.”

What do we know about the hacking?

The accusation came from the FBI, which blamed a state-tied hacking group called TraderTraitor over the weekend.

This was reportedly the biggest crypto-exchange heist on record, well above the roughly $1.5 billion Bybit raid in 2025, which was also attributed to North Korean hackers. TRM Labs linked the attack to the same group and said it shifted most of the money out within 20 minutes, German news agency DPA reported.



Kim Yo Jong said Pyongyang now had "issues to reconsider" because of Washington's hostility.

North Korea has so far stayed silent on Trump's overtures about reviving summit talks. Analysts in Seoul told Reuters news agency the speed of the denial points to concern that Washington could step up efforts to cut off a funding source widely believed to bankroll arms development.

Is Binance working again?

Separately, Binance announced Monday that withdrawals will restart for additional assets across several blockchains, among them Binance Smart Chain, Ethereum, Solana, XRP and Sui, from 04:00 GMT Tuesday.

Selected tokens on Arbitrum, Optimism, Tron and Base are part of the same rollout.

Binance said it replaced most of the stolen assets out of its own funds.
